items.label: September 1938
items.sum: Report on the 1938 Inter-Club Relay Shield contests against Mitcham A.C., Epsom H. and Croydon H., which Belgrave won again with 63 points out of a possible 64.
items.s: The “Inter-Club” Relay Shield Contests. Report on the 1938 Inter-Club Relay Shield contests against Mitcham A.C., Epsom H. and Croydon H., which Belgrave won again with 63 points out of a possible 64. The second in this series was held at Croydon on May 31st, and we fielded quite a strong team and dropped only 1 point out of a possible 16. We won both the 4 x 100 yards and 4 x 300 yards relays, and then after a close and exciting race we also won the 4 x 880 yards. We were not so strongly represented in the 1 Mile team race, and Mitcham proved the winners of this with Bob Thorogood as the individual winner. The points scored that evening were : Belgrave H. 15, Mitcham A.C. 12, Croydon H 8, Epsom H. 5. On 13th July we visited Epsom for the third contest and once again the “turn-out” of our chaps was good to see. Unfortunately the same could not be said for our opponents and Mitcham were very weakly represented. The racing was more or less a procession, with our boys in front, and we won all four events. The points scored were : Belgrave H. 16, Mitcham A.C. 11, Epsom H. 7, Croydon H. 6. The final meeting was held at Mitcham on July 27th, and here again we scored maximum points in winning the four events down for decision. It was a pity that Mitcham did not put up a better fight on their own track, and they really have seemed very apathetic over the season’s contests. As regards Croydon and Epsom, we appreciate the hard fight they have in fielding teams; but from a club of Mitcham’s strength and reputation we expect keen opposition. If they cannot do better than this I am very much afraid their period of triumphs is nearing the end. We once again won the Shield, the final points being : Belgrave H. 63, Mitcham A.C. 46, Epsom H. 24, Croydon H. 20. As the highest possible is a total of 64 it will be seen we dropped only one point throughout the series of contests, a record which will stand for many years, and for which our boys deserve every congratulation. They rallied round in fine style and it was a great pity that our rivals did not take these contests in the same spirit. I trust that next season will see the same fine exciting battles that we have previously had for the possession of the Shield. Bob Thorogood Bob Thorogood individual winner of the 1 Mile team race, Croydon, May 31st Inter-Club Relay Shield Croydon Epsom Mitcham Mitcham A.C. Croydon H. Epsom H.

items.label: September 1938
items.sum: Report on the “Doris” Shield contest at Battersea Park Track on June 15th, won by Belgrave from Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. and Thames Valley Harriers despite a track in very bad condition. Handicap results for the 100 yards, 2 miles walk and 1 mile follow.
items.s: The “Doris” Shield Contest. Report on the “Doris” Shield contest at Battersea Park Track on June 15th, won by Belgrave from Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. and Thames Valley Harriers despite a track in very bad condition. Handicap results for the 100 yards, 2 miles walk and 1 mile follow. This season’s meeting was held at Battersea Park Track on June 15th and, as usual, the track was in a very bad condition. In fact, some of the athletes considered it dangerous to run on, and abstained from competing, which is to be regretted; and when things come to such a pitch as this it is high time the L.C.C. were asked to take this question in hand. The holders of the trophy were the Thames Valley Harriers and after making a very bad start in the 100 yards scratch race, they more or less gave up heart and did not compete in the final event. They took this stand on the condition of the track, and A. D. G. White, the Scottish International runner, was one of their members who refused to run. A. T. Liffen, of Ashcombe-St. George’s, won the 100 yards, with Stan Botwright and Tom Wiley filling the next two places. With the points scoring 6 down to 1 in each event, we thus got away to a flying start with 9 points from the first race. In the 440 yards Eddie Pack refused to risk a breakdown owing to the loose surface; and for an athlete of his build his point of view can be readily understood. Dick Michael made a fine substitute, however, and he ran well to beat Flynn of T.V.H., while Frank Webb sportingly turned out and gained points by finishing 4th. The 2 Miles Team race resulted in an easy win for our team and they actually finished abreast in first position. Our three were : Les Cohen, Tom Carter and Charlie Smart, and their time of 9 min. 56 sec. was very good, bearing in mind the state of the track. For the final event, the 1 Mile Relay, Thames Valley H. did not field a team, and we won after a good race with Ashcombe-St. George’s A.C. The final points for the Shield were : Belgrave H. 30, Ashcombe-St. George’s A.C. 21, Thames Valley H. 12. As usual at this meeting, we had three handicap events open to members of the competing clubs. items.label: September 1938
items.sum: Report on the Kinnaird Trophy meeting at the Polytechnic Harriers' new ground at Chiswick, won by Achilles with Belgrave fifth on 12 points, with Tom Carter second in the Southern Counties 2 Miles Steeplechase, a Belgrave team win in the Invitation 2 Miles Walk and Belgrave finishers in the Marathon.
items.s: The “Kinnaird Trophy” Meeting. Report on the Kinnaird Trophy meeting at the Polytechnic Harriers' new ground at Chiswick, won by Achilles with Belgrave fifth on 12 points, with Tom Carter second in the Southern Counties 2 Miles Steeplechase, a Belgrave team win in the Invitation 2 Miles Walk and Belgrave finishers in the Marathon. We were once again honoured by receiving an invitation to compete at this meeting, which was held at the fine new ground of the Polytechnic Harriers at Chiswick. As usual our boys gave a very creditable display in being placed fifth in the list of competing clubs which included all of any note. Achilles, with their formidable list of talent to draw on—far in excess of any that an ordinary club can command—were easy winners of the trophy with a total of 71 points. Highlights of the meeting so far as we were concerned were Stan Botwright’s fine running in the 220 yards, and in his heat he caused a surprise by beating J. C. Horsfall, of Achilles Club. In the final he was placed 4th, and so scored 3 points. Another fine performance was Eddie Pack’s running in the 440 yards, and after an easy heat win, he made A. G. K. Brown go all the way in the final. Eddie was leading at 300 yards, but once the straight was reached Brown forged ahead, and Eddie was also “pipped” on the tape for second place by C. H. Kearney, the American running for Achilles. It was one of Pack’s best runs to date and if he could only find something of a finish, I would back him against the best in the country. In the 880 yards Alby Bird ran his usual consistent race and although coming up against his “bogey” man, A. D. G. White, in his heat they both managed to qualify for the final. This was a fine race and White proved the winner, just beating J. V. Powell, with Bird in third place. These three runners had so far scored 11 points for us, which was in excess of any number scored previously by us in these contests, and then Charlie Smart, by gaining 6th place in the 3 Miles, brought our totai to 12. At this meeting was held the Southern Counties 2 Miles Steeplechase and although the water jump was far from satisfactory, after some discussion it was decided to hold the race. Tom Carter put up very good and plucky show and after Abberton, of Q.P.H.—he is also a member of the “Bels”—had led most of the way Tom looked like making up the lost ground with a lap to go. Then, bad luck, Tom hit a hurdle and fell and although still retaining second place, he found it impossible to catch the leader. In the Invitation 2 Miles Walk, the Belgrave boys gave the fair sized crowd a good example of the heel and toe “stuff” and Don Brown walked in his best style to beat A. A. Cooper, the A.A.A. champion. Joe Coleman was third, and with Harry Churcher, Percy Wright, Len Coleman and J. E. Rutland giving good support, we scored an easy win in the team race by scoring 13 pts. to Surrey Walking Club’s 39, four aside scoring. In the Marathon, F. A. Walker and A. F. Mitchell ran well to gain first class standards; and Bert Lindsey and F. G. White finished the course and completed our team. Stan Botwright Stan Botwright 4th, 220 yards final (3 points); beat J. C. items.label: September 1938
items.sum: Report of the club 3 Miles Track Championship for the “Griffin” Cup at Battersea Park on June 22nd, won by Tom Carter in 15 min. 12 sec. from the holder Les Cohen, with standard medals, the evening's handicap results, an unattached novices' race and a schools' relay.
items.s: Club 3 Miles Championship Meeting. Report of the club 3 Miles Track Championship for the “Griffin” Cup at Battersea Park on June 22nd, won by Tom Carter in 15 min. 12 sec. from the holder Les Cohen, with standard medals, the evening's handicap results, an unattached novices' race and a schools' relay. At Battersea Park, on June 22nd, we held an evening meeting and included on the programme was our 3 Miles Track Championship for the “Griffin” Cup. The holder, Les Cohen, was among the starters who were quite numerous, although Pat Parker, owing to his domicile, was an absentee. The first mile was reached in 5 min. 2 sec., the second in 10 min. 14 sec., and the leading bunch included all the Club’s most prominent distance runners. Over the final lap Cohen was in the lead with Tom Carter next; and Les still kept in front until half-way down the finishing straight, when Tom made a do-or-die effort, and won a fine race in 15 min. 12 sec. Dan Patience beat Charles Smart for third place, while other runners to gain 1st class standard medals were Rod Patience, Syd Ring, Alf Taylor and Dick Tobin. Second class standards were gained by Afthur Allum, Tom Morrell, R. E. Stride and E. H. Herbert. Also on the programme were several handicap events, and in the 100 yards Junior race R. B. Shepherd (2) beat G. Morgan (3), there being only four starters. The Unattached Novices race, over 100 yards, was won by R. Bradshaw in 11.3 sec. with G. Aylmer and F. Wood next. In the 880 yards race, a Junior in D. L. Mumford (off 72 yards) showed his paces in winning in quite fast time and, as he is finely built, he should prove a most useful addition to our ranks. Syd Jarlett ran a fine race in being second off 28 yards (his improvement this season has been remarkable) and R. J. Powell, off 60 yards, made one of his few appearances on the track, to take third place. We also had a 1 Mile Relay, open to Schools, and were rather disappointed in that only two teams took part in this. Latymer Upper School easily beat Sloane School, to take the first awards, thus repeating last year’s success. I hope that if we hold this event next season we shall gain a much better entry. In the Club Shot Putt handicap, the winner was Frank Webb. Now I know how he gets the nickname of “Snaky,” and he did 37ft. 5½in. with 15ft. start. None other than Percy Wright was second and he did 37ft. 3¾in. off 15ft. 3in., while Joe Coleman was third with 37ft. 0½in. The 100 Yards Veterans’ race was won by J. Smith (6), who beat E. R. Jessop (8), with Dicky Best (7) third. In the 2 Miles Walk an old-time member, in A. H. East, made a return to something like his old form to win off the 550 yards mark. E. G. Cornish (425) was second, with Reg Elson (225) walking well to gain third place. The 220 yards handicap saw R. B. Shepherd win a good race off 16 yards, with Bill Pritchard, off 8 yards, second, and Syd Jarlett (12) gaining another success by being third. The Club Long Jump handicap was won by H. M. Quackenbos (3ft. 6in.) with 21ft. 3in., Charlie Jones and Bill Pritchard gaining the other places. We saw quite a promising runner in the 1 Mile run for Unattached Novices in C. Westwood, who has now joined us. He won in confident style, and should prove a useful addition to our ranks of distance runners. items.label: September 1938
items.sum: Report on Belgrave's win in the Stanley Waddilove Trophy contest at the Birchfield Harriers ground, Perry Barr, on July 23rd, by 13 points to 12 each for London A.C., Blackheath H. and Birchfield H., decided by the final relay on the grass.
items.s: The “Waddilove” Trophy Contest. Report on Belgrave's win in the Stanley Waddilove Trophy contest at the Birchfield Harriers ground, Perry Barr, on July 23rd, by 13 points to 12 each for London A.C., Blackheath H. and Birchfield H., decided by the final relay on the grass. Once again we journeyed to Birmingham to take part in this meeting at the Birchfield Harriers ground at Perry Barr. Last year, at our first time of competing, we managed to share the trophy with the London A.C., but with the Blackheath H. sending up a strong side, which included Sidney Wooderson, we were not too optimistic this time. Further, Eddie Pack was in Belfast running for England in the triangular match there, and so lessened our chance of picking up points in the 440 yards event. Anyway, a very cheerful party under the guidance of our Running Hon. Sec. met at Euston Station on the morning of July 23rd and duly arrived at Perry Barr prepared to do their best. In the 100 yards Ted Gray, as last year, won his heat and so gained a place in the final. Wiard, of Blackheath, as expected, won the final and although close up, Ted was placed 4th, which was not so good as previously. We had a surprise in the 440 yards, inasmuch as both our runners won their heats, and so we had two in the final. Dick Michael and Syd Jarlett were our two stalwarts, but on a very loose track G. N. Blake won for the L.A.C., with Neal and Lansdale, both of Birchfield, in the next two places. Jarlett was inches away in 4th place. Thus we gained another very valuable point and with the 880 yards next, we hoped for the best from Alby Bird. Wooderson made his first appearance in this race and as the field also included J. V. Powell, J. W. Alford (the Empire Games champion) and many other first-class runners, all the crowd were agog with excitement. After a very bumpy start, Wooderson shot to the front and was not again headed, beating Jack Powell, while Alby Bird ran magnificently to beat Alford on the tape for third place. The time of 2 mins. 0.6 secs. came rather as an anti-climax, but no doubt the state of the track coupled with the presence of Wooderson, slowed the field down somewhat. Meanwhile in the centre of the arena the Javelin Throw was proceeding, this event being an innovation as regards this contest. We had Charlie Melchior throwing for us, but with Blakeway and Klein entered for Achilles, our man appeared outclassed. Imagine our surprise when Melchior nonchalantly walked up to us and said he had won the Javelin. It transpired that only three competitors turned out, and these did not include either of the Achilles men, and so Charlie with a throw of 151 ft. beat J. W. P. Ellis, of the L.A.C., with J. Cotter, of Birchfield, next. Thus on points scored we were well among the leaders and our hopes of success were gradually rising. The 2 Miles Team race was next, and although we provided the winning team last year we were much weaker on this occasion. Also the field was a really “hot” one, the Achilles team being Ward, McIntyre and Ellis, while the Poly. had Reeve, Furze and Stockwell, and there were, of course, the Birchfield boys to be considered. Our team, owing to withdrawals, was Charlie Smart, Bill Lucas, Alf Taylor, with our track captain, Harry Shields, making a fourth man. After a very fine race Reeve beat Ward on the post to win a most plucky race in which Ward appeared to make his effort rather late, although I do not think he bargained for the way Reeve fought him off down the straight. Achilles scored 16, to the Polytechnic’s 18 to win the team race, and after much speculation we heard with pleasure that we were third with 32, to Birchfield’s 38. Charlie Smart ran another good race, employing his forcing tactics to take the field along at a good pace, but, as usual, he could not match their pace over the final lap. Bill Lucas, running over his usual distance, did quite well, and Alf Taylor was our third man. So with one event to go we found ourselves in a similar position to last year, We just had to beat the L.A.C. and Birchfield, for the latter were in the lead by one point from ourselves and the L.A.C. As by this time the track was very cut up, the competing clubs asked the officials if they could use the grass for this event. It had been marked out for a previous race, so that it was quite easy to arrange the take-overs, etc., and it was agreed to run on the grass. Sidney Wooderson turned out for Blackheath over the two laps stage, and duly handed over in the lead; but Alby Bird had hunted him home and we were in second place. Syd Jarlett kept us well there and then Stan Blundell went off over the first half lap, and Stan Botwright took over for the final run home. Wiard was leading for Blackheath but Botwright caught him at the bend of the home straight. The Blackheath man was the stronger, however, and beat our runner by a yard or so; with the L.A.C. just beating Birchfield for third place. Oh ! boys ! what a finish ! This had given us the Cup, the final points being : Belgrave H. 13, and then with 12 points came London A.C., Blackheath H. and Birchfield H. Polytechnic H. scored 5, and the Achilles 4 points. Were our lads excited? And it was very gratifying to find the locals were also very pleased at the “Bels” success. After a very nice tea we entrained for home and all that goes with it, and so ended yet another page in the Club’s history—winners of the Stanley Waddilove Trophy ! items.sum: Report of the July 20th match at Battersea Park Track in which Belgrave's Seniors beat Southgate Harriers 42 pts. to 38 and the Juniors won a match against Mitcham A.C., Hercules A.C. and Croydon H, with club handicaps and a Mile Novices Walk on the same programme.
items.s: Match v. Southgate Harriers. Report of the July 20th match at Battersea Park Track in which Belgrave's Seniors beat Southgate Harriers 42 pts. to 38 and the Juniors won a match against Mitcham A.C., Hercules A.C. and Croydon H, with club handicaps and a Mile Novices Walk on the same programme. On July 20th we had as visitors to Battersea Park Track the Southgate Harriers, who met our Seniors in a series of match events. The Milocarian A.C. had also been invited and after accepting, they found at the last minute it was impossible to raise a full team. Actually one of their members came all the way from Portsmouth to compete and was very disappointed at their withdrawal. Our Juniors was also entertaining the junior members of the Croydon H., Hercules A.C. and Mitcham A.C. In the Senior 100 yards Southgate proved too strong for us; but Alby Bird credited us with first place in the 880 yards, and Frank Webb ran a fine race, to gain third place in this event. We had the first two in the Shot Putt with S. Jones and L. J. Worrad; and in the 220 yards Stan Blunden ran a fine race, only to lose first place by inches to S. C. Francis, of Southgate. Another good race was the 1 Mile match and B. S. Cornish, of Southgate, proved the winner, after running a very well-judged race. Bill Lucas chased him home and appeared to have left his effort too late, while Les Cohen filled 3rd position. The 440 yards saw Dick Michael run a smashing race to beat Syd Jarlett, with the Southgate men well in the rear. Points which were scored 4, 3, 2, 1, were equally shared in the Discus Throw, and also the 2 Miles, which E. J. Nankivell, of the visitors, won in good style and quite good time. Thus the Senior match ended with Belgrave H. 42 pts., and Southgate H. 38 pts. The Junior match was also very well contested and some fine running was seen, one of the best performances being J. A. W. Scott’s double in the 100 yards and 220 yards. Scott is quite a “find” for us and should develop into a really fine sprinter. In the 880 yards the winner was J. Emmins, of the Hercules A.C., one of the best juniors in the South and our boys did well in gaining third and fourth places. Our “dusky” member, C. Holloway, gained 4th place in the High Jump and with proper tuition he should do even better. A fine race was seen in the 440 yards and G. H. Knight scored a win for us by battling up the straight to win the race on the tape. D. R. Laing also showed good form in being placed 4th and here again we have two extremely promising young runners. In the final event, the 1 Mile Relay, the Hercules team kept the lead given them by Emmins and our team were also always in second place, the Mitcham boys being third. The points for the Junior match were : Belgrave H. 22, Mitcham A.C. 19, Hercules A.C. 14, Croydon H. 5. Also on this programme were a few club handicaps, one being the 100 yards for Boys under 16. We had quite a good entry and the final was won by A. P.Norris (2), who beat A. V. Heitman (Scr.), with P. Kearney, Jnr. (2) third. In the 2 Miles Walk handicap, A. H. East scored another win, this time off 450 yards, and it would appear his long rest has done him the world of good. W. Brunning, a very persevering member, was second (off 775) and J. Ogilvie (off 500) was placed third. The 220 yards was won by Stan Blunden off 8 yards, with Dick Michael (12) second, and Alec Mewes (11) third. Blunden is another runner to show remarkable improvement this season and if he can only improve his rather ungainly style he should still further increase his speed. In the Mile handicap a good race was seen and although Joe Daly fought hard to keep in front he eventually finished third, with Alf Taylor beating J. T. Beer for first place. The latter has also shewn gradual improvement and now that he is out of the Junior ranks he should soon be knocking at the door of our Senior teams. We also held a Mile Novices Walk, but the entry was poor; although the winner, J. Howard, showed a good style in winning by quite a distance. Alby Bird Alby Bird won the Senior 880 yards v. items.s: The Club Championships. G. S. Doubleday reports the Belgrave club championships at Tooting Bec Track on Saturday, July 30th, with the full results appended; the report puts Bill Sutton third in the Discus behind Worrad and Jones, while the results list W. H. J. Sutton second and S. Jones third, and the report gives Jones’ javelin as 131ft .1in. where the results print 131ft. 1in. These were held at Tooting Bec Track on Saturday, July 30th, on a brilliant summer afternoon; a fair-sized crowd and many club-folk enjoyed the sport. The heats of the 100 yards were held first. Owing to a small field the final of the Boy’s Sprint was held straight away, J. McLean winning from P. Kearney, and A. V. Heitman (holder), in 11.4 secs. Meanwhile, the Shot Putters were “toying” with the 16lb. ball. Sid Jones came out best with an effort of 39ft. 1in. L. J. Worrad and Bill Sutton were 2nd and 3rd, with 37ft. and 34ft. 9in. respectively. No standards (31ft.) were gained here. Then the Juniors lined up for their 880 yards. D. Mumford showed good judgment to win from L. Marchant, and N. Shrubb in 2 min. 7 1-6 sec. This served as an appetiser for the Senior 880 yards, in which Alby Bird (holder) went into the lead at once, with the rest closely behind. At the bell he showed us that he meant to retain his title, and spurted ahead to enter the final straight with a commanding lead to win in 2 min. 3sec. Dick Michael led the others at the last bend and looked as though he would be runner-up, but Sid Jarlett had other ideas, fought him down the straight, and just “pipped” him. Standards (2 min. 8 sec.) were gained by F. H. C. White, F. R. Webb and A. H. Orton. Next came the 100 yards Finals. In the Junior, R. S. Turner won in 10.8 sec., a time which is very encouraging for one under 19. J. A. W. Scott and R. B. Shepherd were 2nd and 3rd. These lads will, I’m sure, soon be forcing themselves into the Club’s Senior teams. In the Senior race, Stan Botwright gained a clear victory in the excellent time of 10.2 sec. over F. Skelley, who was chased home by Tom Wiley. F. Pritchard was the other finalist. The Field Events men had now deserted the Shot for the Discus. This gave us a close finish, Worrad reversing the previous result with Jones (holder) and winning by a foot. Bill Sutton was again third, the distances being 100ft. 7in., 99ft. 7in. and 92ft. 11in. No Standards (85ft.) were obtained. The sprinters were again on the tracks now, deciding who were to line up for the 220 yards final. Our attention was then drawn to the High Jump, which was won by a member whose name is not usually associated with jumping—Eddie Pack. He cleared 5ft. 5in., and a junior, Len Marchant, was second with 5ft. 3in.; he will undoubtedly get higher, as his physique is well suited to this event. H. M. Quackenbos (holder) cleared 5ft. 2in. for 3rd place. The absence of Les Cohen and Pat Parker robbed the Mile of some of its interest, but an exciting race between W. Lucas and L. W. Herbert held the attention of us all. Lucas led the way right from the start, Herbert being content with keeping just behind. Thus they went until the bell, having dropped the rest on the last lap. Herbert attacked down the back straight. Lucas held him for a while, but on entering the final straight Herbert put in a powerful finish which Lucas could not quite resist. This is not only Herbert’s first Club Championship win, but a new Club record of 4 min. 29.2 sec. The field were battling for third place, Charlie Smart proving the best of the bunch. Standards (4 min. 50 sec.) were gained by Dan Patience, Ted Stimpson, Alf Taylor, Tom Morrell, Tom Carter, Harry Shields and Syd Ring. Then the 220 yards finalists lined up and the Juniors again gave us a keen race. In a very good time—23.8 sec.—R. B. Shepherd led R. S. Turner and J. A. W. Scott. Stan Botwright again showed the others a clean pair of heels, winning in 22.7 sec. (new Club record) while A. S. Blunden, F. W. Pritchard and Tom Wiley—finishing in that order—gave us a close race. Eddie Pack, Alec Mewes, S. Lyons and Les Bennett gained Standards (24 sec.) in their heats. In the absence of C. Melchior, G. Powell and E. H. Finneron, the Javelin resolved itself into a close contest between Quackenbos and S. Jones, the former winning with 133ft. 2in. and Jones throwing 131ft .1in. I’m sure that Quackenbos’ prowess is chiefly due to a close study of the finer points of Javelin throwing. A rather small number lined up for the Two Miles Walk. Harry Churcher and Joe Coleman led from the start, with Percy Wright in close attendance until he incurred the Judge’s displeasure. Len Coleman and Bill Treacher were battling for third place until Treacher was disqualified at 1½ miles. Harry was a little too fast for Joe, and won in 14 min. 36 sec. Reg Elson followed home to gain a First Class Standard, but no other Standards were obtained. The holder, D. Brown, did not start, and I am sure that his presence in the race would have added considerable interest. The last race was the 440 yards final. As was expected, Eddie Pack had a comfortable win, and cantered home in 51.6 sec. Sid Jarlett again gave us a fighting finish to beat Alby Bird and Dick Michael. Jarlett’s improved running has been one of the features of the season. A. H. Orton gained another Standard, having beaten 56 sec. in his heat. Meanwhile F. Skelley had jumped 22ft. 8in. to retain his Long Jump title. This is surely one of the best jumps by an Englishman this season. T. D. Wiley and F. W. Pritchard were second and third. No account would be complete without a hearty vote of thanks and a strong recommendation for a big drink and a box of throat tablets for our Hon. Announcer, Arthur Cook, who gave us a sterling performance on the megaphone. Our other officials, too, deserve warmest thanks from both competitors and spectators. Last, but not least, we thank the competitors whose performances will, no doubt, urge them on in quest of greater honours—sufficient unto the day is the attainment thereof. items.sum: Report of the club handicap events at the final evening meeting at Battersea Park on August 10th.
items.s: The Final Evening Meeting. Report of the club handicap events at the final evening meeting at Battersea Park on August 10th. As usual, we held an evening meeting at Battersea Park in August and on the 10th we held the following handicap events. This year we experimented with a 300 yards race, but entries were very poor, due mainly to holidays, and Alby Bird, off 10 yards, ran a good race to just beat Stan Blunden, off 6. Tom Wiley (8) was third while among the also rans was—yes, that man’s here again—Percy Wright. In the Shot Putt “that man,” or in other words, P. G. Wright, was the winner with 38ft. 11in. He received 15ft. 6in. R. Stride, Snr. (16ft. 6in.) did 38ft. 4in., while Alby Bird (15ft. 6in.) gained third prize after dead-heating with the scratch man, S. Jones, both doing 38ft. 3in. As Jones did 39ft. 1in. in our Club Championships, a repetition of this would have gained him first place. A good race was seen in the 880 yards Junior handicap and L. Marchant made good use of his 10 yards allowance to beat N. C. Shrubb (15) for first place. Our Junior champion, D. L. Mumford, was third off the scratch mark. These three juniors are three extremely promising young runners, and Shrubb was recently selected to represent the Surrey Juniors. The 2 Miles Walk saw a rather small field and Charlie Speechley (450) scored a popular win, with A. H. East, off a much reduced mark, still keeping among the prize winners by being second off the 330 yards mark. Reg Elson walked in his usual fluent style to gain third place with 190 yards start. Harry Churcher walked well from the scratch mark and eventually worked his way through to 4th place. A popular distance with our lads is the 2 Miles race and Ted Stimpson showed he is working back to his best form by winning off 100 yards; while Tommy Morrell (160) ran well to gain second place. Frank Webb (170) was third. To Frank it would appear that the distance is immaterial, be it anything from 300 yards to 10 miles. Another feature of this race was the fine running of L. W. Herbert who, off 50 yards went through the field in fine style and only lost third place in the last few strides. He just failed to overtake Frank Webb, and as the time of the race was 9 min. 30 sec., Herbert must have been doing fast time as he was close up to the leaders at the finish. items.s: The Forthcoming Winter Season. Preview of the 1938-39 winter season: training at Belgrave Hall, Wimbledon and the mid-week quarters at the "Rising Sun", Ebury Bridge Road, and the autumn fixtures. The piece ends at the foot of printed page 28 (scan p.30) without a sign-off, but the printed page numbers run unbroken from 1 to 28 and are followed by the blank back covers, so no pages are missing from the scan. After one of our most successful Summer seasons ever, we look forward with confidence to the forthcoming Winter season. We have arranged a full fixture list and I trust our members will give the fixtures their fullest support, both at home and away. We are also extremely fortunate in possessing our own hall—Belgrave Hall—at Wimbledon and here again the Common is ideal for running purposes. I hope all members, both new and old, will come along to Wimbledon and sample the delights of a run over the country, there is nothing better for getting rid of that “tired” feeling, never mind what the advertisements say! We have a fine bath of hot water for use after the run, and our capable masseur, Tom Easton, is also in attendance, if required. Saturday runs always start about 3 p.m. and for those who would like to do some mid-week training we have our quarters at the rear of the “Rising Sun,” Ebury Bridge Road, which is quite near Victoria Station. We go out from here every Tuesday and Thursday evening and run over the adjacent roads into Hyde Park, when we go round Rotten Row, which makes for very useful country training, especially if we have had some rain, and then back to the quarters. Hot water can also be obtained here and while conditions are not quite so ideal as at Wimbledon it must be borne in mind that suitable mid-week quarters, especially in this vicinity, are extremely difficult to obtain. Now a word as to our fixtures. On the first Saturday in October (which is October 1st) we hold our annual 3 Miles Road Run and 5 Miles Road Walk. Both these events are handicap races and all members have an equal chance of success, so be sure to enter in good time. The following week, October 8th, we hold the usual Novice races open to Unattached men, and also members of our own Club. If you have any friends who would like to try their paces, bring them along to Wimbledon on this day. We are then away to Ealing Harriers, and then on the 22nd we have a home fixture with London University C.C.C. In conjunction with this race we shall hold our usual 5 Miles handicap. We expect to have a good field out. This season we visit Cranford for the annual Inter-Club race with Thames Valley H. and Ashcombe-St. Georges A.C., the date being October 29th. Then on November 5th we make our first visit to Aldershot for a run with the Aldershot Command team. We are also paying a visit to Cambridge for a run with the University Hare and Hounds and in each case a picked team will represent the Club. items.s: The Hon. Secretary's Commentaries. The secretary's notes on the vote of thanks to W. L. Bayliss on his retirement as Hon. Secretary, the club's answer to a press claim that athletics was unknown in Wimbledon, members' marriages, the R.W.A. 20 Miles team in the Lord Mayor's Show, Harry Churcher's walking form, cross-country hopes and the Winter Handbook. Every member will endorse the Vote of Thanks which was accorded to W. L. Bayliss at the Annual General Meeting, when he announced his retirement from the office of Honorary Secretary. It was framed in the following terms, proposed by W. H. Hare :— “That this meeting place on record its very grateful thanks and appreciation for the services rendered to the Belgrave Harriers by Mr. W. L. Bayliss as the Hon. Sec. during the past eleven years. His unfailing efforts to further the development and welfare of the Club in all its activities have materially assisted in the acquisition of every Road and Cross Country Team Honour in the Athletic World. In addition, his services have been of the greatest assistance in obtaining the leasehold of our own Headquarters. We feel that no Hon. Secretary has retired with as great a measure of satisfaction of service rendered to our Club and we both congratulate and thank most heartily Wally Bayliss for his sterling efforts on our behalf.” A. A. Harley said that such a proposition required no seconder but was rather the expression of feeling of every member present, and upon formally placing the motion before the meeting it was received and passed with acclamation. As President of the Club for the third successive year, we are assured that there will be no diminution in his interest, or in his labours on the Club's behalf. His experience gained in close upon twenty years' membership of the Club will still be ours to draw upon, and his enthusiasm for all aspects of the Club's activities will remain an example to all members. * * * * * We note from the Press that a Wimbledon Athletic Club has been formed, and shall watch its progress with interest. Naturally, we take the broad view and welcome any new organisation likely to bring newcomers into the ranks of Athletics, and extend the influence of our sport among a new section of the public. We must confess, however, to some slight annoyance at reading the “blurb” which appeared in one of our national papers and accompanied the announcement of the formation of the new club. From this it would appear that Wimbledon has only been known hitherto in sporting circles by reason of its association with Lawn Tennis. No doubt the Royal Wimbledon Golf Club and Wimbledon F.C., to name only two sporting bodies, would be inclined to dispute this; and we certainly think we have some claim to have brought some small Athletic distinction to the Borough of Wimbledon. For many years now we have been privileged to train at Wimbledon, and it would be no exaggeration to say that the Cross-country and Road Walking titles we have gained have been won, in part, on the Common and roads of Wimbledon, in advance of the Championship events. On nineteen occasions we have promoted an Open Walk at Wimbledon, attracting an average entry of 200 walkers. Last season we invited French athletes to Wimbledon for the first time ever, as far as we know, and the Mayor and members of the Corporation honoured us by officiating at these events and congratulated the Club upon its efforts for Athletics. We are minor property owners and ratepayers in Wimbledon, and our quarters have been at the disposal of the Wimbledon “Keep Fit” movement and other sporting organisations—and yet we are told that Athletics is an unknown sport in Wimbledon! So much for Press reports. We are content to carry on in a placid way, doing what we can for athletes and Athletics, wherever we can, achieving Championship honours or failing honourably to do so; and leave the verdict to those who have an intimate knowledge of all the facts, and ignore the inaccurate vapourings of ill-informed hearsay. * * * * * Congratulations to C. W. Redgrave and F. H. C. White upon their recent marriages. We wish both these popular members many years of happiness. * * * * * The appearance in the recent Lord Mayor's Show of the winning team in the R.W.A. 20 Miles Championship and the Hon. Secretary—representing Road Walking—was an honour to the Club. These five members paraded in Club track suits in the Athletics section of the National Fitness Campaign pageant, which was the central motif of this year's Show. * * * * * Harry Churcher is again showing his heels to all other walkers. We congratulate him upon the excellence of his form, and trust he will be equally successful in the races still to come. Our teams are also pre-eminent at the moment, and we confidently anticipate that their series of successes will continue. * * * * * Our runners are training steadily and showing up well in inter-club events, and are certain to give a good account of themselves when the Championship season arrives. Every club member hopes the team will be free of injury and indisposition during the coming months, and successfully bid for the English Cross-country Championship next March, to be held near Manchester. * * * * * All members should now have their Winter Handbook containing Winter fixtures and Rules. Anyone who has not received his copy should get into touch with the Hon. Secretary. * * * * * W. L. Bayliss W. L. Bayliss retired as Hon. items.label: December 1938
items.sum: Letter from A. A. Harley, editor since April 1929, wishing the new editor luck and thanking F. R. Webb and E. A. Duffett for their support.
items.s: Letter from A. A. Harley, editor since April 1929, wishing the new editor luck and thanking F. R. Webb and E. A. Duffett for their support. 39, Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. Dear Mr. Editor, May I trespass on your space to wish you the Best of Luck with “The Belgravian,” and plenty of support from all members in the position to which you have been appointed by the Committee? It was in April, 1929, that I succeeded Ben Knifton as Hon. Editor, and during the intervening years I have had the pleasure of presenting 59 issues to an increasing membership, and have had the honour of recording Belgrave victories in practically every team championship and race of any importance. I trust it will be your good fortune to continue to record success after success, and to give written expression to the wonderful spirit within the Club that has created these successes and the good-fellowship which is so real to all of us. In conclusion, I should like to thank all who have co-operated with me during the past nine years in my Editorial efforts, particularly F. R. Webb and E. A. Duffett, two stalwarts who have always given me invaluable support. I am sure that we may expect many fine “Belgravians” under your direction, and that we shall all eagerly await each quarter the results of your labours. And so, good editing! Sincerely yours, A. A. HARLEY. A. A. Harley A. A. HARLEY Hon. Editor from April 1929, 59 issues Ben Knifton Ben Knifton Hon. Editor before April 1929 F. R. Webb F. R. Webb E. A. Duffett E. A. Duffett Isleworth

items.label: December 1938
items.sum: The new Hon. Editor introduces himself, invites members' articles alongside sectional reports, and notes that A. A. Harley will continue to contribute.
items.s: From The Hon. Editor. The new Hon. Editor introduces himself, invites members' articles alongside sectional reports, and notes that A. A. Harley will continue to contribute. Having been appointed by the Committee to be Editor of your magazine, I feel that I would like to write a few words in my first issue. I write “your Magazine” because it is your magazine, written about you and for you, and it is by no means an unimportant phase of the Club's activities with which I must confess a little pride in being associated. I don't think that any other athletic club can lay claim to a publication of the size of “The Belgravian.” However, being what we are (if you don't know that, I will ask you to turn to the letter from A. A. Harley, in which he sums the Club up in a few well-chosen and appropriate words), the publication of this organ possesses the fullest justification. With the aim of placing on record the performances of all sections of the Club, I have obtained the willing co-operation of the sectional officials, who will produce their reports and views. This, of course, does not bar any member from submitting articles—in fact, they will be most welcome, for then it will be you writing your magazine, and I know articles by someone who was on the spot have a wide appeal amongst the Club fellows. My predecessor, A. A. Harley, will still contribute in the form of “General Honorary Secretary's Notes,” and it is hoped he will continue that popular feature “Ten Years Back.” This is greatly appreciated by our newer and younger members. In conclusion, I might add that any suggestion or criticism will be very gratefully received. With the co-operation of the Club officials, to whom I must again record my deepest appreciation, I have the greatest hope of attaining in some measure the high standard set up by my predecessors. A. A. Harley A. A. Harley previous Hon. Editor

items.label: December 1938
items.sum: Report of the Annual General Meeting of 27 September 1938: 46 present during the crisis, accounts adopted, J. R. McKay and T. Cotton made Life Members, W. L. Bayliss re-elected President and succeeded as Hon. Secretary by A. A. Harley, and the new captains named.
items.s: The Annual General Meeting. Report of the Annual General Meeting of 27 September 1938: 46 present during the crisis, accounts adopted, J. R. McKay and T. Cotton made Life Members, W. L. Bayliss re-elected President and succeeded as Hon. Secretary by A. A. Harley, and the new captains named. Belgrave Hall, 27th Sept., 1938. The President, W. L. Bayliss, presided, 46 members being present. the smallness in numbers being due to the crisis. The Hon. Secretary read the notice convening the meeting. The minutes of the last A.G.M. were read and confirmed. The Hon. Secretary then reported on the past year's activities. He commented on the good form of the cross-country teams, the improvement shown in Field Events and on the Track, and the exceptionally successful year enjoyed by the walkers. He hoped that the International situation, then menacing, would clear, and that the Club would again have a most successful year. This was accepted with acclamation. J. R. McKay (Hon. Auditor) read a written report of the accounts, the Hon. Treasurer having sent a letter regretting his absence. The reports were adopted on the proposal of F. G. Thomson, L. G. Bennett seconding. On behalf of the Committee, A. A. Harley proposed that .J R. McKay and T. Cotton be elected Life Members. He outlined the exceptionally good services that both these members had rendered the Club over a number of years. This proposal, when put by the President, was carried unanimously. The proposal by J. R. McKay that W. L. Bayliss should again be President was adopted with acclamation. W. L. Bayliss announced his retirement from the position of Gen. Hon. Secretary after eleven years, in which he had served the Club to the best of his ability, and seen the Club victorious in every Cross-Country and Road Walking Championship. He now thought that another member should carry on in this office, and announced that the Committee had considered the matter and that A. A. Harley was willing to allow his name to go forward on the assurance that he would receive the fullest co-operation. E. A. Duffett formally proposed and A. W. Penny seconded that A. A. Harley should be General Hon. Secretary, and the motion was adopted accordingly. The other officials were then elected as they appear in the new Handbook. The captaincies show a few changes. Bert Footer takes charge over the country again. He will be helped by Arthur Penny and Bert Lindsay. This is a new post for the latter. His steady running, knowledge of the courses and popularity should enable him to fill this post successfully. If versatility is the essence of a Track Captain, then we could have made no better choice than Frank Webb, whose experience and knowledge of our track runners should enable him to carry the Club on to further honours. He will have the co-operation of our new Field Event Captain, Charlie Jones, who is only a shade less than he is in versatility. From these deliberations I am sure that we will face the coming season with well justified optimism. W. L. Bayliss W. L. Bayliss President; presided; re-elected President; retired as Gen. Hon. items.label: December 1938
items.sum: Report and full result of the club Three Miles Road Race handicap on 1 October 1938 over a new hilly course, won by Lionel Penny from N. C. Shrubb, with Arthur Penny fastest in 15 mins. 5 secs.
items.s: The Three Miles Road Race. Report and full result of the club Three Miles Road Race handicap on 1 October 1938 over a new hilly course, won by Lionel Penny from N. C. Shrubb, with Arthur Penny fastest in 15 mins. 5 secs. 1st October, 1938. This year a different course was used. Instead of going out to the Windmill and home via that rough road across the Common and through the village, a lap of the hills was done. The actual times of the runners would suggest that the course is a little longer than the old one. Our old friend, George Still, started first, the last to start was Arthur Penny, who, although not on the scratch mark, gave proof of his fitness by clocking 15 mins. 5 secs. to record the fastest time. A. W. Jerman give us a good performance, being second fastest. The first to arrive was Lionel Penny, who was followed home by our promising junior, N. C. Shrubb. Then came our old friend, Bert Lindsey, to whom this race must have seemed like a sprint after his marathon efforts. Bert Smith was fourth. No doubt this will urge him on in his next handicap to gain those few seconds and so gain a place. Lionel's win was, no doubt, a great satisfaction to Arthur, whose years of experience, and his proven ability, enable him to give much useful brotherly advice. As regards the result as a whole, well, nobody can really expect fast times from everybody; some are fit, whilst others use this race as a loosener for the more serious work to come. RESULT. Pos. items.label: December 1938
items.sum: Report on the two three-mile road novice races, open to Belgrave and unattached novices, which brought in new members.
items.s: Novice Races. Report on the two three-mile road novice races, open to Belgrave and unattached novices, which brought in new members. These races were open to both Belgrave and unattached novices and were both held on the road over three miles. They were instrumental in bringing us new members, which is, after all, the object of them. Many of the competitors gave useful performances, which they will soon be improving on if they are given the necessary encouragement and training. It is now up to them, for they have now only to report to their respective captains or vice-captains. We welcome them to the Club and wish them every success in their future races.

items.label: December 1938
items.sum: F. A. Walker's report of the season's first cross-country race, against Ealing H. from the Ballot Box, Perivale, won easily by Belgrave with A. R. Shaw first home; the printed result skips 14th place and its team scores do not match the club letters in the list.
items.s: Run v. Ealing H.—15th October. F. A. Walker's report of the season's first cross-country race, against Ealing H. from the Ballot Box, Perivale, won easily by Belgrave with A. R. Shaw first home; the printed result skips 14th place and its team scores do not match the club letters in the list. By F. A. Walker. Our first cross-country race of the season was against Ealing H. from their headquarters, the Ballot Box, Perivale. The team we sent was a strong one—good enough to win a "National"—if all were fit! The course was a fairly fast one. The Ealing fellows got away very fast at the start, having about a dozen men in the lead for the first three-quarters of a mile. After that they faded away one by one, then our lads had a "social" run amongst themselves. About two miles out we came across a miniature Everest which we had to climb, and what a climb! A. R. Shaw was the first man home, closely followed by six more Bels.; then two Ealing lads came in to split up the rest of our boys from the leaders. As we had the next five home we ran out easy winners. items.s: Match v. London University A.C. Report of the race over the club's 5 miles course at Wimbledon on 22 October against London University A.C., run with a club sealed handicap, led home by Arthur Penny, Bert Footer and Dan Patience. H. M. Quackenbos was second London man; A. T. Harper won the handicap; full club placings follow. The text names A. E. Smith third in the handicap where the table prints A. Smith. On Saturday, October 22nd, at Wimbledon, we entertained the members of the London University A.C. to a race over our 5 miles course. They were using this fixture as a trial for their runners, while we had our club sealed handicap in conjunction, so that a field of about 85 turned out. As most of our seniors were running they naturally soon went to the front, and eventually a small bunch of 3 runners drew away from the rest of the field. These were Arthur Penny, Bert Footer and Dan Patience. In the run home Arthur just beat Bert, with Dan third. We then had 10 more more "Bels" before the first London man, who was Alonzo, a member of the Blackheath Harriers. The second London man was none other than our own Junior Captain, H. M. Quackenbos. For the purpose of team scoring we deleted all our seniors, and this made W. E. Lucas—who was actually 7th in the race—first home, with G. Murdock and Tom Morrell next. We were easy winners on points, but trust our opponents enjoyed their run over our course. Our club handicap was won by A. T. Harper, who finished 20th in the actual race, and with 4-20 start he returned a net time of 27m. 27s. M. F. Edwards was second, his net time being 27m. 32s. Third place was taken by A. E. Smith. whose net time was 27m. 40s. We were pleased to see our prospective South of Thames Junior teams running well to the fore, and a newcomer in V. L. Green showed promising form. He comes to us from the Portsmouth A.C. and we hope he will enjoy his membership with the "Bels." Jimmy Kemp also displayed good form and we hope that he will retain it throughout the season, as so often Jimmy begins the season well and then fails to make our teams when the real "tests" come along. It was also good to see George Still "still going strong" (no pun), and even at his time of life he managed to beat a few of the young' uns. items.s: Match v. T.V.H. and Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. October 29th. A. S. Lindsey's report of the five-and-a-half-mile match at Cranford against T.V.H. and Ashcombe-St. George's A.C., where "A" men paced prospective South of the Thames juniors and Belgrave won by a big margin. Ashcombe took the first three places but were third; the result lists club letters and team scores as printed (Belgrave's nine places add to 102, not the printed 82; the results list jumps between 34 and 37 out of order). By A. S. Lindsey. The fact that over 30 of the Bels. travelled to Cranford for this fixture shows that it is still as popular as ever. There was an extra interest in the race, as a scheme by the Cross-country Captain, whereby an "A" team man took charge of two prospective "South of the Thames" juniors for the purpose of team packing and keeping an even pace throughout the race was tried out. From the finishing positions of many Juniors, it can be seen that the scheme had a good deal of success. Especially in the case of Rispin, who ran strongly all the way to finish in the first dozen. Owing to some "A" men not turning out, Footer had more than his share of men to take along. At one stage of the race he looked like a pocket size standard-bearer going into action, surrounded by a high wall of stalwarts. The five and a half miles course was a two lap one, mainly flat grassland with about three-quarters of a mile of woods. Ashcombe led the field home with the first three men, but were third in the team race, nine a side scoring. Although our "A" men were concentrating on getting their charges along they all packed well and we enjoyed a big margin win. Nutty Penny gained a medal given by the home club for being the first scoring man of the visiting teams. RESULTS. TEAM SCORES. Belgrave H. (4, 6, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17) ... ... ... 82 pts. items.label: December 1938
items.sum: "Ubiquitor's" lively account of the race across the Aldershot Command sports fields on 5 November, with forty starters of whom ten were Belgrave Harriers. Dan. Patience won from Hutchings of the Command and Belgrave won 102—108.
items.s: Match v. Aldershot Command—Nov. 5th. "Ubiquitor's" lively account of the race across the Aldershot Command sports fields on 5 November, with forty starters of whom ten were Belgrave Harriers. Dan. Patience won from Hutchings of the Command and Belgrave won 102—108. By Ubiquitor. On the afternoon of the hottest November day for 97 years, forty starters raced across the well manured sports fields of the Aldershot Command and it is slightly to be regretted that only ten were Belgrave Harriers. In the opening rush black vests were well to the fore, but when the runners turned down Golf Lane, Frank Webb jumped to the lead to remind us that once he could show us the way round. But that was before the advent of youngsters like Arthur Penny & Co. It was here the runners picked up the famous "Aldershot horse" that acts as guide, and Jerman went ahead and collected a short lead all to himself. The field was very bunched, with black shirts (vests, I mean) all over the place. After about a mile, Jerman fell back and Kemp led a tight pack for a while along a road, until Charlie Smart decided that the road was obviously made for speed, and speeded. Jimmy Kemp thought it over and decided to help him along, so he moved up as well, but for the next couple of miles could not make up his mind whether he was running with Charlie Smart in the lead, or with Hutchings of the Command or even whether he was defintely third. But at half-way these three had a sixty yard lead from Dan. Patience, followed by a nasty black patch. Then came Arthur Penny in a sweater, trying to "kill" a cold and looking like a grease spot. Tobin had caught Frank Webb and they were having a regular argument, because Tobin could run uphill and no one can catch Frank going down, and the course was full of short, sharp ups and downs with a real pull here and there. Behind were Syd Ring and Verney, who was just settling down, Jerman and good-natured Alex Patience, who took upon himself the thankless task of being last man in the team. With about a mile to go the first three were fighting a ding-dong battle for the lead, when Dan. Patience evidently thought that someone should show how to run—and passed the lot! Hutchings hung on best and was rewarded with a second place. Kemp and Smart came in "all friendly like." Then there was a black outlook, slightly lightened by by Arthur's white sweater. Then, fortunately, Bels. showed they also could pack. With Verney running through to 11th, Ring pipping Tobin and Webb for 12th, Tobin (13) doing the dirty on Webb (14) (a real Knifey finish), Jerman (17), and Alex Patience (19) beating the last scoring Command man. All 10 men scored, and we won by the sporting margin of 6 points, 102—108, and admitted over an eggs and bacon tea that the race was good. The tea was very good and the sight of a sweat-covered and lathered horse gave a satisfaction not ordinarily enjoyed after racing. RESULTS. Belgrave H. items.s: South of Thames Junior Race. Report of the South of Thames C.C. Association's annual Junior Team race at Dartford on 12 November, with 34 teams and 243 runners, four of the teams Belgrave. Herne Hill Harriers won; Belgrave's "B" team was 4th and "A" team 7th after two "A" men blew out; teams and team positions follow. Tom Morrell is named in the "A" team but not in the printed team lists. On the 12th November the South of Thames C.C. Association held their annual Junior Team race at Dartford. 34 teams faced the starter, and four of these were representing the "Bels." There was a field of 243 runners and they made a fine sight streaming across the country. Unfortunately our "A" team were drawn on the extreme outside, and owing to the spectators encroaching at the start they found themselves badly away. Bill Lucas soon worked his way into the first half-dozen runners, but the others were always fighting hard to get through the large field. It was a course of three laps, and as this included a fairly steep hill, it was not exactly an easy run, but a good feature from our point of view was that practically all our men gained ground each lap. This was especially noticeable in the final lap, but unfortunately their fine efforts proved to be in vain. We had 7 runners in the first 31 home in the race, and when it will be seen that Herne Hill Harriers won the team race with their fourth man scoring 34th, it must be wondered why we had no team placed in the first three. Well, it all resolved upon that very ticklish question, "team selection." As stated, we had four teams entered and our "B" team beat the "A" while E. H. Herbert, who was actually in the "C" team, finished 27th and beat all but two of the "A" team. All the talking in the world will not alter the result now, but to put the matter frankly, it was a question of two of our "A" team men, namely, V. L. Green and Tom Morrell, "blowing out" while our "B" team actually ran above all their previous form and so put the "cat among the pigeons." Whatever the team result, we can console ourselves with the fact that our Juniors proved themselves the best of any other club, and as most of them are young in years, as they grow older and gain more experience we can look forward to the future of our senior teams with every confidence. Below you will find the result in detail, and we have put the runners in team order with their actual positions and times beside them. RESULT. TEAM POSITIONS. 1 Herne Hill H. e: Belgrave v. Cambridge University Hare and Hounds
items.s: Match v. Cambridge University Hare and Hounds. November 19th. Harry Shields' report of the new fixture against Cambridge University Hare and Hounds on a 7½ mile course from their headquarters on the Cam, which Cambridge won 30 pts. to 52 against seven Belgrave men, Dan Patience finishing second to D. C. Chamberlain; the printed Cambridge placings add to 29, not the printed 30. By Harry Shields. It was a pity that for this new and attractive fixture only 7 men, with Harry Parker as team manager, could manage to make the journey. However, it was a cheerful party that met on Liverpool Street Station and caught the train to Cambridge, where they were met and escorted to the University's headquarters on the bank of the River Cam. The course consisted of one 7½ mile lap containing about 3 miles of plough and two hills and as can be well imagined, was a good testing course. Getting off to a very fast start, the Cambridge men for the first mile were predominant but after settling down Dan Patience went up with the leaders whilst Tom Carter, Alf Shaw and Harry Shields also occupied prominent positions. The plough, however, soon proved the fitness of the Cambridge men—enabling them to run out easy winners as shown below. The result, however, is far from discouraging, bearing in mind the time of the year, the far heavier defeats that Cambridge have inflicted on other teams, and the fact that we were far below full strength. Dan Patience's running against D. C. Chamberlain, admittedly one of the fittest men in England, bore the mark of International honours to come. Tom Carter shows a gradual return to form, whilst the running of Herbert and Quackenbos, both of whom have done very little training, was very creditable and points to them being very useful team members in the New Year. An excellent tea wound up a pleasant afternoon with a sincere hope from all that this enjoyable fixture will be long continued. RESULTS. Cambridge U. (1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9)... ... ... 30 pts. Belgrave H. items.label: December 1938
items.sum: H. E. F.'s exhortation to younger cross-country members to keep training and racing through the winter after the South of Thames Junior race, as a foundation for the track season.
items.s: In Terrorem. H. E. F.'s exhortation to younger cross-country members to keep training and racing through the winter after the South of Thames Junior race, as a foundation for the track season. There is a feeling among the younger members of the Cross-country Section of the Club, that once the South of Thames Junior race is over their season has finished. This is a fatal mistake. For instance, when you are transferred from one class at school, or one department at business, to another—can you sit back and take things easy? No! You have to jump to it! To concentrate, to study, and work hard to maintain that position. Therefore, to those of you who aspire to become potential track champions, don't slacken off now, or those joints will become rusty again. Keep fit! Keep training and you'll find, as the season progresses, you will desire to go faster and further than any previous years over the country. All of you can safely race at least once a month over seven miles up to February, and then indulge in some long steady spins before reverting to the track, as no serious work on the track can be done until the light evenings come round, which is time enough to think about speed work, etc. Give yourself a proper preparation—get stamina—which means strength of limb, muscular development of stomach—and wind—that is, lung capacity, using the chest to its utmost, all of which hard running over the country enforces you to do whether you want to or not. Don't forget that your time and facilities for training are limited, whereas when the time arrives for serious work, the Service and University type of athlete can train for hours nearly every afternoon in the best conditions, while you rush your training through in those brief few hours of the evening. Study the records. you will find that many track champions have also shone over the country—Sydney Wooderson and Reg. Thomas are two such—and remember that strength and speed make the champion every time. Some of you can make it! Who is it going to be? Those who have come off or those who this time have failed? You all have an equal chance, but it will require "guts." So to it, you fellows! H. E. F. H. E. F. H. E. F. signed the piece Sydney Wooderson Sydney Wooderson example of a track champion who also shone over the country Reg. Thomas Reg. items.s: Ten Years Back. Column recalling club happenings of ten years earlier from the Gazette: triangular matches with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley H. at Feltham and Wimbledon, the South of the Thames Junior win at Epsom, open walks and club championships. Let us have a peep at the happenings of ten years ago. Our Gazette of this time records the results of one of the triangular matches between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and ourselves, held at Feltham. We were successful with 77 points, to 275 of Ashcombe and 276 of T.V.H. Percy Bicknell, of the Valley, was the individual winner, followed by Cohen (Ashcombe) and Mick Pyer (Belgrave). Three weeks later a similar fixture was held at Wimbledon over a five miles course, and ninety runners finished. First man home was Cohen (Ashcombe) with Footer (Belgrave) second, and J. E. Flower (Belgrave) third. Once again we had an easy win in the team race, and the sealed handicap was won by S. Drake (3m. 15s.) with H. E. Footer (15sec.) second. Belgrave entered four teams in the South of the Thames Junior race held at Epsom, and our "A" team gained an easy win. It consisted of W. W. S. Mitchell (2), A. Penny (3), A. Allum (4), and W. A. Rice (13), and our enthusiasm was high. The first Open Walk of the season, promoted by the R.W.A. attracted 231 starters and we were successful in winning the scratch team race and "Berman" Cup. The Belgrave Open Walk had 246 entrants, and the scratch team race resulted in a dead heat between Herne Hill Harriers and ourselves with 41 points each. Our team consisted of T. W. Green, J. G. Scammell, R. D. McMullen and F. H. Elson The Club Junior Walking Championship for the "Horwood" Cup was won by Frank Elson, J. E. Field and J. Rathbone finishing second and third. The Seven Miles Cross-country Championship for the "Backstaffe" Shield was won by E. A. Duffett, with A. Allum and W. G. Webb in the minor positions. These were the happenings of ten years ago! items.label: December 1938
items.sum: E. A. Duffett's preview of the club's winter fixtures, from the Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park through the county, South of Thames and Southern championships to the English C.C. Championship at Worsley on March 11th.
e: South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championship
items.s: Forthcoming Fixtures. E. A. Duffett's preview of the club's winter fixtures, from the Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park through the county, South of Thames and Southern championships to the English C.C. Championship at Worsley on March 11th. The half-way stage of the Winter season has already been reached, although the big races have yet to come. This, of course, is as it should be; for with the gradual strengthening process, our runners should now be approaching that stage when they feel fit to take on all and sundry. The only possible snag is that with all the races taking place in the New Year, it is a question of the "cracks" indulging in races almost every other week. Only the very fittest can expect to stand up to this strain, and so it is essential to do the long steady training, which although at times may seem irksome, is the only way to reach the front rank of runners in the cross-country world. As a break from all this country training, we have on Boxing Day morning, at Battersea Park Track, a club track meeting starting at 11 a.m. There are three events, all on handicap lines, these being: 120 yards, 2 miles Run, 3 miles Walk. These are usual races at this meeting, which is very old-standing, and we must judge by the entries we receive as to whether our members still wish this meeting to continue. It may seem strange to some that we have a sprint event at this time of the year, but we have several sprinters out every Saturday from Wimbledon, and these men at any rate must be in a fair state of fitness. As to the other races, I am sure most of our distance men will welcome the break to shorter distances, and although they may be a little lacking in speed, remember it is a question of everyone being in the same "boat," so don't forget to enter and come along and enjoy yourselves on the "morning after the night before." After the holiday period is over we get back to our cross-country fixtures, and on December 31st we have the pleasure of welcoming the Junior members of the Blackheath H. and Old Croydonians H. This should give our junior members a chance of measuring their chances in regard to the coming Junior Championships, and I trust we shall have a good turn-out for this race. On January 7th we have the County Senior Championships, and the Surrey race is being held from the quarters of the Ranelagh H. at Petersham. This should prove a good cross-country course, and I look to our men to reverse their position with the Mitcham boys of last season. Now that the latter's Welsh members have acquired a residential qualification, it will be seen that our lads are faced with stiff proposition, more especially as our forces have to be split in these County races. Our members who run for the Cadogan A.C., in the Middlesex race proved to be winners last season, and we trust they will carry on the good work, and, on his present form, Dan Patience should go very near for individual honours. On January 14th we are staging the Surrey County Junior Championship from the "Belgrave Hall" at Wimbledon. Our 5 miles course will be used, and on their own "midden" I hope our juniors will succeed in carrying off team honours; while in E. H. Herbert we have a youngster who should trouble the best in the race. I would like to ask as many old members as possible who are free on this day to come along and give us a hand in staging this race, as many pointsmen will be needed, owing to the ban on laying a paper trail over the Common. On January 28th we are holding the Club 10 miles C.C. Championship at Wimbledon, while this season we are also holding the Club 5 miles Junior Championship on the same day. These will be two separate races, our 5 miles course being used in each case, with the Juniors doing one lap and the Seniors two. In conjunction with the senior race we shall have a Club sealed handicap, so I hope that all our members will support this race, as no matter what their position in the race, they should all stand a chance for the handicap (at least, this is what the Handicapper says). On February 11th there will be held the South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championship, and the venue for this will be Camberley. It is intended to use the R.M.C. quarters for dressing accommodation, so that all the runners should have no grouses in this respect, although this is not always the case with cross-country races. Then on 25th February we have the Southern Counties C.C. Championships at Apsley. This is near Hemel Hempstead and the palatial quarters of Messrs. John Dickinson & Co. Ltd., will be used to house the hundreds of competitors. There will be two races, the Senior race over 10 miles and the Junior race over 5 miles. At this stage of the season we can only hope for the best, but we have the men and if "Dame Fortune" will only smile on us for once, I am sure we can come out on top. I trust that Pat Parker will be at his peak by then, and with Art Penny, Bert Footer, Dan Patience and Tom Carter, to mention just a few, surely we are justified in feeling confident that we shall regain this championship, which we last held in 1934. We come then to the English C.C. Championship which will this year be held in the North, the venue chosen being at Worsley, near Manchester. As usual with these Northern venues, I expect the course to be a tough one, and I hope that as many of our supporters who can spare the time to make the journey will do so. Our boys will need all the vocal encouragement that they can possibly get. So make a note of this date, March 11th, and do your utmost to travel up to Manchester with our boys. No doubt a special train will run from London, and full details of this will be given at a later date. All entries and enquiries to— E. A. Duffett, Running Hon. Sec., 76, Greenside Road, W. Croydon. items.sum: W. H. J. Sutton's field events notes: Wednesday evening training at Wimbledon under F. Stampfl, a Boxing Day match against the Metropolitan Police, S.A.A.L. results and S. Jones winning the Harry Wright Shield.
items.s: Field Events. W. H. J. Sutton's field events notes: Wednesday evening training at Wimbledon under F. Stampfl, a Boxing Day match against the Metropolitan Police, S.A.A.L. results and S. Jones winning the Harry Wright Shield. By W. H. J. Sutton. The evening training at Wimbledon on Wednesdays is going strong, averaging about fourteen members each session. The Club has purchased a medicine ball, two gym. mats, a High Jump bar, and a twelve-pound shot, and Alf Taylor has made a hurdle for indoor training. Under the training of F. Stampfl, the session starts with a one and a half miles warm-up round the Common, then about thirty minutes' strenuous exercises, followed by Hop-step-and-jump and High jumping, and instruction in the different technique for each event. Another Field Events match against the Metropolitan Police at Battersea Park on Boxing Day has been arranged. T. C. Jones, the Field Events Captain, will notify the men selected for the teams. The events are Discus, Javelin and Shot. The complete S.A.A.L. results now issued show that we have obtained 24 out of 69 of the first three places in the 23 events held, showing our individual performances, as well as team results, to be among the best. S. Jones has won the Harry Wright Shield for his excellent performance in the Shot—39ft. 1in. It is possible that the rules governing this competition will be rearranged to be based on the Finnish table of calculation which was used for the Olympic Decathlon. Enquiries to T. C. items.sum: H. M. Quackenbos's notes on the junior section: cross-country form and prospects in the junior championships, then a look back at a successful junior track and field season.
items.s: With The Juniors. H. M. Quackenbos's notes on the junior section: cross-country form and prospects in the junior championships, then a look back at a successful junior track and field season. By H. M. Quackenbos. So far this season very satisfactory form has been shewn by our cross-country men, and Beard, Shrubb and Herbert deserve special mention for their good running in the South of the Thames Junior Of the various junior championships our chances seem most favourable in the Surrey. We have a potentially strong four, including Boyden, in addition to the three above, and it will be surprising if we can't win the title, especially as the race will be held over familiar country from Belgrave Hall. The Southern Junior team will be weakened because Herbert and Boyden will be too old, but fortunately Edwards and Bradnum come in here. Lomas, Marchant and Scarfe represented us in the Surrey Youths' race and finished in position 21, 22 and 23. The first-named is a very keen newcomer who will do very well when he matures. Now for a word about the Track (and Field) season, which should have been mentioned in the last issue but wasn't, and on whom the blame rests only I know. Anyhow it was a most successful season and, if memory serves me, we won every match except one. The most gratifying thing, however, was the enthusiasm shown and at a match at Richmond, so many men turned up that they all could not be given a run, although would-be half-milers turned out in the sprint relay. Turner, Scott, Bowers and Shepherd formed a sprint relay team which was placed in both Southern and A.A.A. Junior Championships. Turner and Scott have both been close to 10.5 sec., while Shepherd has beaten 24sec. in the furlong and does a good quarter as well. Knight always runs a strong race in this latter event and with perseverance and a more relaxed style he should soon be doing about 53 seconds. In the half, Mumford, Marchant and Shrubb have all been running about 2min. 8 sec. and Reynolds hasn't been far behind. In the mile Bradnum has beaten 4min. 45sec. and has gained another standard medal in the A.A.A. junior steeplechase. Lastly, our two Field Events men, Butcher and Holloway, have been joined by a talented recruit, Harvey, who at the age of thirteen has jumped 4ft. 11in. Dunford and Cooper have both tried long jumping, with some success, but our star in this event, Peverell, had the misfortunte to break his ankle early in the season. items.s: 5 Miles Handicap (Walk). 1st October, 1938. Report and full result of the club 5 miles walking handicap on 1st October 1938 over a slightly altered course, won by H. G. Churcher (Harry Churcher) from scratch. The field for this was not as large as it might be, as most of our Police stalwarts were unable to turn out. The limit man, W. Brunning, started off up Lauriston Road, followed by the rest at varying intervals. A slight alteration was made in the course and this new course will be used in future races and training spins. Instead of turning left at Woodhayes Road, keep straight on along Ernle Road. This road bends to the left and joins Copse Hill; turn right and proceed as usual. This route shortens the course slightly. Brunning kept in front until Cambridge Road, when Charlie Speechley and Eddie Heather went into the lead. At the top of the hill Harry Churcher went in front and went on to win by over half a minute. This performance shows us that Harry means business in the coming "opens." Harry Thaxter and Charlie Speechley had a ding-dong battle down Lauriston Road for second place, Thaxter gaining the verdict by a very small margin. RESULT. H'cap Time. Allce. Act. Time. 1 H. G.
