items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Article comparing performances using the I.A.A.F. scoring table of 1934, ranking world records and A.A.A. standards by points.
items.s: Who's Best ? Article comparing performances using the I.A.A.F. scoring table of 1934, ranking world records and A.A.A. standards by points. Some interesting results emerge from a study of the Scoring Table for Track and Field Events as adopted by the I.A.A.F. Congress at Stockholm in 1934. This table, in addition to giving a means of scoring for Decathlon competitions, satisfies the curiosity of those who would like to know, for example, if a hundred in "evens" is better than a quarter in 49 seconds. Looking up the former, we find that it scores 872 points whilst the latter obtains 954 points, so that the quarter is better. A scale of points is given for all metric running distances, except the steeplechase and marathon; and for all the Field Events, including the standing jumps. The points range from 1360 down to 1 by intervals of one point. Opposite each number the corresponding performances, in the different events, are listed. The compilers have catered for everyone, from the superman of many years hence, who will run 800m. in 1 min. 41.5 sec., to score 1360 points, to the champion of the kindergarten, who toddles round the metric half mile in 3 min. 17.6 sec., thus getting one point. Arranging the world's records in order of merit, we find that the Field Events occupy most of the leading positions with Jack Torrance's shot putt of 57ft. 1in. topping the list and scoring 1202 points. If it has been adopted as a world's record, Owen's 20.3 sec. for the 200 metres is the best pure running performance. The middle and long distance records are in the lower half of the list. Wooderson's 800 metres record is worth 1109 points as against 1088 due to Lovelock's 1500 metres in Berlin. Rather surprisingly the "worst" record is the 10,000 metres recently put up by Maki, which scores 1075 points. Coming nearer home, to A.A.A. standards, we discover, as expected, that the running events score consistently higher points (about 840 on the average) than the Field Events, which average 670 points. The influence of cross-country running is shewn by the fact that the most difficult standard to obtain is the three miles (14m. 50s.) which, converted to 5,000 metres, scores 884 points compared with the easiest, the discus (120ft.), which obtains 613 points. In fact, excepting the high and long jumps, the man who wins an A.A.A. standard in a Field Event does not put up quite so good a performance as he who attains Middlesex county standard in any running event. It must be realized that this table is true only if the performances are done under standard conditions (say ideal conditions) and makes no allowance for wind, heavy or loose track, etc. To compare one running performance with another or a Field Event with another Field Event, the table can be used with confidence, but the comparison of a track record with a field record does not give such good results. From the above facts it appears that in the region of World's records the running events do not score enough points while in the part of the table corresponding to A.A.A. standards, the Field Events, even allowing for their low rating in England, should be given more credit. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Report of the club's Boxing Day Christmas Social, with tea, dancing and a members' performance of "Little Nell".
items.s: The Christmas Social. Report of the club's Boxing Day Christmas Social, with tea, dancing and a members' performance of "Little Nell". This was held on Boxing Day, and some 90 odd members and friends sat down to a hearty tea. Then came a bout of dancing, a little breathing-space followed, during which some of our dramatically-inclined members gave us their version of "Little Nell." The following gentlemen formed the cast—let their names speak for themselves! F. A. Walker—the Father—complete with beard (and how it shook when he laughed!), Wellington boots and other clothes which looked as though he was just off on a Polar expedition! A. A. Bird—Little Nell (a little fast, perhaps, but she does a 1.59 "half"). She wore black shoes and stockings, a pale yellow shirt which hid a sausage balloon. Evidently the "Pidge" did not wish to give the impression that she lacked maternal affection. C. T. Carter—the Policeman, complete with coat and helmet, trundling a toy tricycle around—and who can blame him for deserting his running legs in these mechanical days? Besides, his mount added to the dignity and poise of authority. P. G. Wright—the Villain. Percy undoubtedly knew his villains well, for he was rigged up in evening dress, collar and bow, and spats. He tried to disguise himself by hiding behind a moustache, and by smoking a cigar (real) completed the picture of wanton dissipation. Suffice it to say that, notwithstanding a few "divertissements" such as the Lambeth Walk, their acting was powerful enough to send the audience into hisses and boos ("booze?"). A band was engaged and Bill Sutton operated a radio amplifier. Even this did not render Bill free from the sudden (but well-calculated) embraces of one of the ladies, who, after careful manœuvering, caught him unawares. A frame-up is strongly suspected. After the interval, when cries of "Where's the M.C.?" (Les Bennett) had died down, Bert Footer, dressed up as a jockey and mounted on his bucking steed, Syd Jarlett, gave us a quick Rodeo act. They were faithfully followed by Micky Walker in the rôle of stable-boy. Thus the party amused itself until it broke up at 11-30. Everybody voted the party a success, and it seems to have found a place in our Social calendar. Although not run for profit, a balance on the right side resulted. Finally, mention must be made of the good work of our Social Committee who, working under our popular Hon. Social Secretary, Tommy Morrell, were responsible for a most enjoyable evening. To them we all express our warmest thanks and gratitude. F. A. Walker F. A. Walker played the Father in "Little Nell" A. A. Bird A. A. Bird played Little Nell C. T. Carter C. T. items.h: The Lighter Side of the Club.
items.sum: Social notes on the loss-making second dance at Zeeta House, the coming Social on March 25th, and the Annual Dinner and Dance at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on May 6th.
items.s: The Lighter Side of the Club. Social notes on the loss-making second dance at Zeeta House, the coming Social on March 25th, and the Annual Dinner and Dance at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on May 6th. Unfortunately, the success of our first Dance at Zeeta House was not maintained at the second. In an effort to prevent overcrowding our Social Sub-committee did not use their high-pressure salesmanship in disposing of the tickets. As a result the Dance showed a loss, many regular Club members not appearing on February 11th. Now, come, boys! Do not leave it to outsiders to make these dances successes. I'm sure everyone present had an enjoyable time, including our Cross-country Captain who, between dances, made repeated dives to the Bar. Looking through some old issues of the "Belgravian," I see mention of a Club record made at a social on November 22nd, 1930. The report is very interesting. Firstly, that 140 sat down to tea on this occasion and secondly, that we had two vocalists, both members of the Club (Tom Cotton and Billy Williams) who sang old favourites with great success. Now, the purpose of our Social, on March 25th, is to break this very old record, also to discover talent, which I am sure still exists among the many members of the Club. In the old days we had such artists as Bill Williams, T. Cotton, "Castor and Oil," the Nonesuch Girls and the Belgrave Sisters, to mention only a few, who were always willing to oblige for the enjoyment of those present. The chance is yours! Now see what you can do to brighten our Socials in the future. You will receive full support from the Social Sub-committee. Do not be afraid to make any suggestion if you think that it will make our socials sucesses! * * * * * I would like to bring to your notice the Club's Annual Dinner and Dance which, this year, is to be held at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on Saturday, May 6th. Although this date seems a long way off, I ask you all to make a note of it, and to make your reservations as early as possible. With your co-operation, the Social Sub-committee hope to make this the Social Event of the year. Tickets will cost: Single 6/-, Double (lady and gent.) 11/6. Everything possible is being done to ensure a function worthy of the Club. Members wishing to use instalment cards for the payment of Dinner Tickets should get in touch with me as soon as possible—the strictest privacy will be assured in this matter. * * * * * For any further Social particulars, please apply to T. F. Morrell, Social Hon. Sec.. 3, Florian Road, S.W.15. items.sum: Short notes on the club's junior cross-country runners, praising the Junior Championships winner, Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter, and urging juniors to start track training.
items.s: With the Juniors. Short notes on the club's junior cross-country runners, praising the Junior Championships winner, Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter, and urging juniors to start track training. Our junior runners have given plenty of evidence of their ability during the present season; and we have every confidence that they will also be prominent in Track events this coming Summer. Herbert has been our best man this season, and deservedly won the Junior Championships, but Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter deserve mention as a more than useful recruit and for great improvement respectively. The others, whose form is well known, have all shown improvement on last season. Perhaps I can best conclude these short notes with the warning that the track season is almost upon us and an exhortation to non-cross-country juniors to start their training with plenty of long, slow work, preferably with the sprinters' pack from Belgrave Hall on Saturday afternoons. items.sum: Notes for the club's marathon runners on the coming season: the Finchley 20 miles, a likely Surrey race and the Poly's Windsor to London marathon, with their standard medals.
items.s: Marathon Notes. Notes for the club's marathon runners on the coming season: the Finchley 20 miles, a likely Surrey race and the Poly's Windsor to London marathon, with their standard medals. During the last two seasons we have entered teams for this type of race. That these teams have always been in the first three shows that this little band is already attaining the high standards set by our other teams. By the time that these notes appear our marathon runners will be starting training on the road. For those who do not fancy the full 26 miles, there is the Finchley Harriers open 20 miles race, with a team race held in conjunction. The Surrey County A.A. will probably be holding a similar race. Standard medals are awarded in each race. In the Finchley race it is 2 hours 15 mins.; in last year's Surrey race it was calculated on the winner's time. What it will be this year remains to be seen. Later on comes the Poly's classic race from Windsor to London (Chiswick). Last year three Standards were awarded, viz., 3 hours, 3 hours 15 mins. and 3 hours 30 mins. This gives the more moderate performers a chance to gain a medal. Even if one fails to gain a Standard and finishes the course, there is the satisfaction of having done the distance, and the urge to train on to a better performance. Experience counts a great deal, and a certain amount of experiment is needed to adapt one's pace and style to suit the longer distance. In this connection the writings of Arthur Newton can be studied with advantage. Well, if these notes have attracted any potential "pavement pounders," and if further information is desired, the following will be at Wimbledon on Saturdays until May: F. G. Ford, A. S. Lindsey, A. F. Mitchell, F. A. Walker and F. G. White. Any member who would like to join the pack for one lap (eight miles) is cordially invited to do so. In conclusion, I might add that much useful advice can be obtained from our old friend George Still, who was a first-class marathon runner during the early part of this century. items.sum: Preview of the London to Brighton Relay and the Club 5 miles road race, complaints about Battersea Park Track, and lists of the club's track fixtures and the open meetings for the coming season.
items.s: Forthcoming Fixtures. Preview of the London to Brighton Relay and the Club 5 miles road race, complaints about Battersea Park Track, and lists of the club's track fixtures and the open meetings for the coming season. The Cross Country season is now drawing to a close and our thoughts are turning towards the London to Brighton Relay Race. On March 25th at Wimbledon we hold our Club 5 miles Road race, with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. I hope we shall see a good field out for this race, and there is bound to be a rare old tussle for the leading places, as our "Brighton" team is selected after this race. The day of the Relay is Easter Saturday, April 8th, and the start will be from Mitcham, as last year. Our rivals from Mitcham will be out for blood, as another victory this year will see them equal our record feat of three wins in succession. I expect the Birchfield boys to put up their usual good show, but if Mitcham are to be beaten then it is up to the "Bels." to do the trick. Our team should be as good as last year, when although only finishing third, I think it is generally agreed that but for our bad luck on the second stage, and seeing the way our lads ran on the subsequent stages (especially Harry Verney on the third and Pat Parker over the final leg), given ordinary luck this time we shall be right there. There is always the chance of a runner breaking down, but for it to happen again this year is not to be thought of, and so I can see no reason why we cannot this time turn the tables on our conquerors. A few words about the coming Track season may be of interest to our members, and as usual the bulk of our meetings will be held at Battersea Park Track, which I hope the L.C.C. will put into much better condition than last season. I agree that this track is probably the most used of any London one, but a little foresight on the Parks Committee's part could help this "old dust-heap" regain a little of its former fine running surface. Meetings are held there every day of the week and hundreds of school children use the ground, but surely if the track was closed from 5 p.m. to 6-30 p.m., and some attention given to it, the surface would not be as it is at present. However, I suppose we must hope for the best and so I give a list of our fixtures to be held during the coming season :— We have again arranged to hold the Club Championships at Tooting, as this venue proved popular with our members last season. The fact of it being rather late was due to no fault of ours, as this was the only date that the L.C.C. could offer us. We had asked for a date in June, but were unable to obtain one, and so had to accept August 5th, which, no doubt, some members will recall was always the day fixed for the Club Championships in the past. This is the Saturday before August Bank Holiday, and I hope that our members will take note of the date, and, if possible, arrange their Summer holidays, if any, accordingly. I have also been able to ascertain some of the other "Open" dates, and so that members can make a note of these, I have asked our Editor to allow me to append the following list of meetings :— In addition to the above, we hope to arrange several Inter-Club matches both for Seniors and Juniors; these will be given on our Summer fixture card, which will be issued when our fixtures are completed. Thus it will be seen that our members will be kept busy during the Summer, and if any new members are desirous of any further information I shall be pleased to assist them.
